chapters.n: Micah came from Moresheth, a farming town in Judah’s foothills. He prophesied about 740–700 BC, the same era as Isaiah, to both capitals: Samaria in the north and Jerusalem in the south.

f.g: His name means “Who is like Jehovah?” — a question echoed in Micah 7:18.
From Moresheth-gath, about 25 miles (40 km) southwest of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Like a court summons, Micah calls all people and the whole earth to hear, with the Lord Himself as witness from His heavenly temple.
The Lord is pictured stepping out of heaven and striding across the earth’s heights. When God comes to judge, creation reacts.

f.w: the LORD cometh forth out of his place

f.g: Mountain heights — and also the hilltop shrines where idols were worshiped.

chapters.n: Mountains melt like wax near fire and valleys split open like water rushing down a slope. No power can stand before God.

f.w: the mountains shall be molten under him

chapters.n: Why does He come? Because of Israel’s sins. The capitals themselves, Samaria and Jerusalem, have become the centers of corruption.

f.g: Here the northern kingdom, Israel.
Shrines for false worship; Micah says Jerusalem itself has become one.

chapters.n: Samaria will be reduced to a heap of rubble, fit only for planting vines. Its stones will tumble down the hillside. Assyria destroyed it in 722 BC.

f.g: Uncover, lay bare.

chapters.n: Samaria’s idols will be smashed. Their wealth, gained through spiritual “prostitution” (unfaithfulness to God), will be carried off as plunder to pay other idolaters.

f.g: Wages — here, the gifts given at pagan shrines.

chapters.n: Micah grieves openly. He goes barefoot and stripped like a mourner or captive, crying like jackals and ostriches in the desert.

f.g: Jackals.
Ostriches, known for their mournful cries.

chapters.n: Samaria’s “wound” cannot be healed — and it is spreading to Judah, right up to Jerusalem’s gate. Assyria’s King Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC.

f.w: he is come unto the gate of my people

chapters.n: Micah begins a lament full of wordplays on town names along the invasion route. “Tell it not in Gath” echoes David’s lament for Saul. In Beth-aphrah (“house of dust”), roll in the dust.

f.w: Declare ye it not at Gath

f.g: Beth-le-aphrah means “house of dust.”

chapters.n: Shaphir (“beautiful”) will go into exile in shameful nakedness. Zaanan (sounds like “come out”) will not come out. Beth-ezel’s mourning means it can offer no support.

f.g: “Beautiful town” — its beauty becomes shame.
Sounds like Hebrew for “go out”; its people dare not go out.
Perhaps “house of nearness/support.”

chapters.n: Maroth (“bitterness”) hoped for good, but disaster from the Lord reached Jerusalem’s gate.

f.g: Means “bitterness.”

chapters.n: Lachish, Judah’s great fortress city, is told to harness horses to flee. It was where Israel’s sins first took root in Judah — perhaps by trusting chariots instead of God.

f.g: Its name sounds like rekesh, “steed.” Sennacherib’s siege of Lachish is pictured in famous Assyrian wall carvings.

chapters.n: Judah will give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath, Micah’s hometown, as it is lost. Achzib (“deceit”) will prove deceptive to Israel’s kings.

f.g: Farewell gifts or dowry — like giving away a daughter.
Sounds like akhzav, “deceptive brook” — a stream that dries up.

chapters.n: Mareshah (“possession”) will get a new possessor — a conqueror. Israel’s glory (its nobles) will hide in the caves of Adullam, where David once fled.

f.g: A conqueror who takes possession.

chapters.n: Shave your heads in grief, as bald as a vulture, for your beloved children are going into exile.

f.g: Cut off your hair.
Probably a vulture, whose head is bare.

chapters.n: Woe to those who lie awake plotting how to cheat others, then carry it out at dawn simply because they have the power to.

f.w: it is in the power of their hand
f.g: They do it because they can.

chapters.n: Powerful landowners seize fields and houses from ordinary families. In Israel land was a family’s God-given inheritance, so this robbed future generations too.

f.g: Inheritance — the family land God promised could never be permanently sold.

chapters.n: The schemers have “devised” evil; now God devises disaster for them. They will wear a yoke they cannot shake off and will no longer walk proudly.

f.g: The same word as “devise iniquity” in verse 1 — God answers their plans with His own.
Escape the yoke — slip your necks out of it.

chapters.n: Their enemies will mock them with a song of lament: “We are ruined! He has handed our fields over to traitors!” The land-grabbers will lose their land.

f.g: A taunt song.
To an apostate or a captor.

chapters.n: No one in their family will be left to receive a share when the land is divided again by lot.
The people tell the true prophets, “Don’t preach! Don’t talk about these things — disgrace won’t overtake us.”

f.g: Literally “drip” or “drool” — a scornful word for preaching.

chapters.n: Micah answers: Has the Lord’s patience run out? Is this what He wants? God’s words do bless those who live uprightly.

f.g: Restricted, impatient.

f.w: do not my words do good

chapters.n: Lately God’s own people act like enemies, stripping the coats off peaceful travelers who feel safe.

f.g: Returning from war, or peaceable — not expecting attack.

chapters.n: They evict widows and mothers from their homes and rob children of their God-given inheritance forever.

f.g: The blessing and dignity God gave them — their place in the land.

chapters.n: “Get out! This is no place of rest.” The oppressors who drove others out will themselves be driven out, because their sin has polluted the land.
If a liar came preaching about wine and beer, he’d be just the prophet these people want. People prefer messengers who tell them what they want to hear.

f.w: I will prophesy unto thee of wine and of strong drink

chapters.n: A sudden turn to hope: God will gather the remnant of Israel like sheep into a fold. Latter-day Saints see this as part of the promised gathering of Israel.

f.w: I will surely gather the remnant of Israel

f.g: An Edomite region famous for sheep.

chapters.n: “The breaker” — one who breaks through barriers — leads the flock out through the gate, with their King and the Lord at their head. Many Christians see Christ as this Shepherd-King who opens the way.

f.g: One who breaks open a way, like a shepherd breaking through the fold wall.

f.w: their king shall pass before them

chapters.n: Micah addresses Israel’s rulers. Shouldn’t they, of all people, know what justice is? Leaders are responsible for fairness.

f.g: Justice.
Leaders, judges, and officials.

chapters.n: Instead they hate good and love evil. Micah uses a shocking image: they skin the people alive.

f.w: Who hate the good, and love the evil

chapters.n: Like butchers, they chop up God’s people and cook them in a pot. The image shows how they consume the poor for their own gain.

f.g: A large cooking pot.

f.w: eat the flesh of my people

chapters.n: When disaster comes, they’ll cry to the Lord, but He won’t answer. Those who ignore the cries of the poor will find their own cries unheard.
False prophets mislead the people. They preach “peace” to anyone who feeds them, and declare war on anyone who doesn’t.

f.g: Have something to chew on — when they are fed.

chapters.n: Their spiritual light will go out. Night will fall on them; they’ll receive no visions or answers.

f.g: Practice divination — seek hidden knowledge by occult means.

f.w: the sun shall go down over the prophets

chapters.n: These seers and diviners will be humiliated and cover their mouths like mourners, because God gives them no answer.

f.g: A gesture of shame or mourning (Leviticus 13:45).

chapters.n: In contrast, Micah is filled with power from the Lord’s Spirit, with justice and courage to name Israel’s sin. True prophets speak by the Spirit, whether popular or not.

f.w: I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD

chapters.n: Micah again calls out the leaders who despise justice and twist what is right.

f.g: Make crooked everything that is straight.

chapters.n: They build Jerusalem’s grand buildings with blood and injustice — through forced labor and exploitation.
Judges take bribes, priests teach for pay, and prophets tell fortunes for money — yet they claim, “The Lord is with us; nothing bad can happen.” Religion has become a business.

f.w: the priests thereof teach for hire
Is not the LORD among us?

chapters.n: Because of these leaders, Zion will be plowed like a field and the temple hill overgrown like a forest. A century later, elders saved Jeremiah’s life by recalling this prophecy and how Hezekiah repented.

f.w: Zion for your sake be plowed as a field

f.g: The temple mount.

chapters.n: After the destruction of 3:12, a glorious reversal: in the last days the Lord’s temple will be lifted high above all mountains, and people will stream to it. These verses (1–3) are nearly identical to Isaiah 2:2-4, quoted in 2 Nephi 12.

f.w: the mountain of the house of the LORD
f.g: Latter-day Saints often apply this to temples, including the Salt Lake Temple in the tops of the mountains.

chapters.n: Nations will urge one another to go up to God’s house to learn His ways. God’s law and word will go out from Zion and Jerusalem — two centers of truth.

f.w: he will teach us of his ways
the law shall go forth of Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem
f.g: Latter-day Saints sometimes read this as two world capitals of the Lord’s kingdom in the Millennium.

chapters.n: The Lord will judge among nations and settle disputes. Weapons will be turned into farming tools, and war will end. This describes the peace of the Millennium.

f.w: they shall beat their swords into plowshares

f.g: Knives for trimming grapevines.

chapters.n: Micah adds a homey picture Isaiah doesn’t: each family resting under its own vine and fig tree, with nothing to fear. Peace means personal security and enough to live on.

f.w: every man under his vine and under his fig tree

chapters.n: Other nations may follow their gods for now, but we will walk in the name of the Lord forever. A personal commitment of loyalty.

f.w: we will walk in the name of the LORD our God

chapters.n: In that day the Lord will gather the lame, the outcasts, and those He had disciplined. God’s kingdom welcomes the wounded.

f.g: The lame, limping one.

f.w: I will gather her that is driven out

chapters.n: The weak will become a remnant, and the scattered a strong nation. The Lord Himself will reign from Mount Zion forever.

f.w: the LORD shall reign over them in mount Zion

chapters.n: Jerusalem, the watchtower of the flock, will receive back its former kingdom and dominion, as in David’s days.

f.g: Hebrew Migdal-eder — a lookout tower for shepherds near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:21).
The former kingdom, as under David and Solomon.

chapters.n: Back to the present: Why are you crying out? Do you have no king or counselor? Jerusalem is in agony like a woman in labor.

f.g: In labor, giving birth — pain that leads to new life.

chapters.n: Jerusalem must suffer exile — leave the city, live in the open field, and go to Babylon. But there the Lord will rescue her. Micah foresaw Babylon over a century in advance, while Assyria was the great power.

f.w: thou shalt go even to Babylon
there the LORD shall redeem thee

chapters.n: Many nations gather against Zion, eager to see it desecrated.

f.w: let our eye look upon Zion
f.g: Let us gloat over her.

chapters.n: But they don’t know the Lord’s plan: He is gathering them like sheaves onto a threshing floor to be judged. The Savior quoted verses 12–13 to the Nephites.

f.w: he shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor

chapters.n: Zion is told to rise and thresh like an ox with iron horns and bronze hoofs. The spoils of the nations will be dedicated to the Lord of all the earth.

f.w: Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion
I will consecrate their gain unto the LORD

chapters.n: Jerusalem is under siege and humiliated: enemies strike Israel’s ruler on the cheek with a rod. Christians also see a foreshadowing of how the true Judge of Israel, Jesus, would be struck.

f.g: Jerusalem, pictured as a city of soldiers — or one now gashing itself in grief.

f.w: smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek

chapters.n: One of the Bible’s clearest messianic prophecies: from little Bethlehem will come Israel’s Ruler, whose origins are “from everlasting.” The chief priests cited this verse to Herod, and it was fulfilled in Jesus’s birth.

f.g: Bethlehem in the district of Ephrathah, David’s hometown, about 6 miles south of Jerusalem.

f.w: out of thee shall he come forth

chapters.n: Israel will be given up to enemies until “she who is in labor” gives birth — then the scattered brothers will return. The birth points to the coming Messiah.

f.w: she which travaileth hath brought forth

chapters.n: This Ruler will shepherd His flock in the Lord’s strength and majesty. His people will live securely, for His greatness will reach the ends of the earth.

f.g: Feed = shepherd.

f.w: great unto the ends of the earth

chapters.n: “He shall be our peace.” When invaders come, God will raise up more than enough leaders to repel them. “Seven… eight” is a Hebrew way of saying “plenty.”

f.w: this man shall be the peace
seven shepherds, and eight principal men
f.g: A numerical pattern meaning “more than enough.”

chapters.n: These leaders will defeat Assyria, “the land of Nimrod.” The Assyrian here stands for every great enemy of God’s people.
The scattered remnant of Jacob will be a blessing among many nations, like dew and gentle rain from the Lord — refreshing, and coming by God’s timing, not man’s.

f.w: as a dew from the LORD

chapters.n: But the same remnant will also be like a lion among sheep. The resurrected Savior quoted this verse twice to the Nephites, applying it to the latter days and the remnant of Jacob in the Americas.

f.w: as a lion among the beasts of the forest

chapters.n: God’s people will triumph over their enemies.

f.w: Thine hand shall be lifted up

chapters.n: Then God will remove the things His people trusted instead of Him — first horses and chariots, their military might. The Savior quoted verses 10–14 in 3 Nephi 21.

f.w: I will cut off thy horses

chapters.n: He will remove fortified cities and strongholds — false securities.

f.w: throw down all thy strong holds

chapters.n: He will get rid of sorcery and fortune-tellers, which tried to get guidance apart from God.

f.g: Fortune-tellers.

chapters.n: Carved idols and sacred pillars will be destroyed. People will stop worshiping things they made with their own hands.

f.g: Sacred stone pillars used in pagan worship.

chapters.n: He will uproot the Asherah poles — wooden symbols of a fertility goddess — and destroy the cities devoted to idolatry.

f.g: Hebrew asherim — wooden poles honoring the goddess Asherah.

chapters.n: Finally, God will bring justice on the nations that refuse to obey. The Savior added “who have not heard” in 3 Nephi 21:21, connecting it to those who reject His latter-day work.
The scene becomes a courtroom. The Lord tells Micah to present His case, with the mountains and hills as the jury.

f.g: Argue a legal case.

chapters.n: The mountains — ancient witnesses that have seen all of Israel’s history — are called to hear the Lord’s lawsuit against His people.

f.g: A lawsuit or legal dispute.

chapters.n: God speaks tenderly as the injured party: “My people, what have I done to you? How have I burdened you? Tell me!” His love is wounded, not merely His authority.

f.w: O my people, what have I done unto thee?

chapters.n: God reminds them of His saving acts: freeing them from slavery in Egypt and giving them leaders — Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

f.w: redeemed thee out of the house of servants

chapters.n: Remember how King Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, but God turned the curse into blessing — and how God brought them from Shittim across the Jordan to Gilgal. These memories show God’s faithfulness.

f.g: Saving acts — God’s faithful deeds.

chapters.n: Now the people respond with questions: How should I come before God? With burnt offerings of the finest year-old calves?
The questions escalate absurdly: thousands of rams? Rivers of oil? Even my own firstborn child? People sometimes think they can buy God’s favor with outward offerings.

f.g: Child sacrifice was practiced by Israel’s neighbors and condemned by God (2 Kings 16:3).

chapters.n: Micah’s great answer: God has already shown what is good — act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God. This summarizes true religion in one sentence.

f.w: to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love and kindness.

chapters.n: The Lord calls out to Jerusalem. Wise people fear His name. Pay attention to the “rod” of discipline and to the One who sent it.

f.g: Or “fears your name.”
Heed the coming punishment.

chapters.n: Are there still treasures gained by fraud in the houses of the wicked, and dishonest, short measures? God hates such cheating.

f.g: A shrunken ephah — a grain measure made smaller to cheat buyers.

chapters.n: Can God call people innocent who use rigged scales and bags of false weights? Honest business is a matter of holiness.
The city’s rich are violent and its people are liars.
So God will strike them and make them sick and desolate because of their sins.

f.w: make thee sick in smiting thee
f.g: Or “I have begun to strike you.”

chapters.n: They will eat but stay hungry; they’ll try to save things but fail, and what they save will be lost to war. These are covenant curses from the law of Moses.

f.w: Thou shalt eat, but not be satisfied

chapters.n: They will sow but not harvest, press olives but not use the oil, make wine but not drink it.

f.w: Thou shalt sow, but thou shalt not reap

chapters.n: They follow the wicked practices of Kings Omri and Ahab — the northern kings famous for Baal worship and injustice. So they will become a ruin, mocked by others.

f.g: An object of scorn — people whistle or hiss at it.

chapters.n: Micah laments that searching for a good person is like looking for fruit after the harvest — nothing left but disappointment.

f.g: The few grapes left after the harvesters pass through.
Early figs, a prized delicacy.

chapters.n: Faithful people have vanished. Everyone lies in wait to harm others, hunting even their own relatives with nets.

f.w: The good man is perished out of the earth

chapters.n: Officials and judges demand bribes, and powerful people get whatever they want. They all scheme together.

f.g: They weave it together — conspire.

chapters.n: The best of them is like a briar or thorn hedge — they only hurt. But the day the watchmen warned about is coming, and confusion will seize them.

f.g: The prophets who warned of judgment.
The time of God’s judgment.

chapters.n: Society is so broken you can’t trust friends, advisers, or even your spouse.

f.w: keep the doors of thy mouth
f.g: Guard what you say.

chapters.n: Families are torn apart — children against parents. Jesus quoted this verse to describe how His gospel would divide some households.

f.w: a man's enemies are the men of his own house

chapters.n: But Micah turns from despair to faith: “As for me, I will look to the Lord and wait for the God who saves me. My God will hear me.” A turning point for any discouraged heart.

f.w: I will look unto the LORD
I will wait for the God of my salvation

chapters.n: Speaking for Zion, Micah tells the enemy not to gloat: “When I fall, I will rise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord will be my light.” Hope survives defeat.

f.w: when I fall, I shall arise
the LORD shall be a light unto me

chapters.n: Zion accepts the Lord’s discipline because she has sinned, but trusts He will later take up her cause and bring her into the light. Repentance includes owning our sins and trusting His justice.

f.w: I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned
he will bring me forth to the light

chapters.n: The enemy who mocked, “Where is your God?” will be shamed and trampled like mud in the streets.

f.w: Where is the LORD thy God?

chapters.n: A day is coming to rebuild Jerusalem’s walls, and its borders will be extended far.

f.g: Better: “the boundary shall be extended.”

chapters.n: In that day God’s people will stream back from Assyria, Egypt, and everywhere — from sea to sea and mountain to mountain.

f.g: Possibly “Egypt” (Hebrew matsor).

f.w: he shall come even to thee

chapters.n: Yet first the earth will be desolate because of the deeds of its inhabitants.
Micah prays: Lord, shepherd Your people with Your staff. Let them graze again in the rich pastures of Bashan and Gilead, as in the old days.

f.w: Feed thy people with thy rod

f.g: Fertile grazing lands east of the Jordan, lost to Assyria.

chapters.n: The Lord answers: as when I brought you out of Egypt, I will show you wonders again. The Exodus is the pattern for future deliverance.

f.w: According to the days of thy coming out of the land of Egypt

chapters.n: The nations will be stunned and humbled when they see God’s power. They will cover their mouths, speechless.

f.w: lay their hand upon their mouth

chapters.n: Proud nations will crawl in the dust like snakes, trembling as they come out of hiding to submit to the Lord.

f.w: lick the dust like a serpent

chapters.n: Micah’s closing hymn plays on his own name (“Who is like Jehovah?”): Who is a God like You, who forgives sin and delights in mercy? God’s anger is temporary; His love is lasting.

f.w: Who is a God like unto thee
f.g: An echo of Micah’s name, Mi-ka-yah, “Who is like Jehovah?”

chapters.n: God will again have compassion; He will trample our sins underfoot and hurl them into the depths of the sea — gone forever. A beautiful picture of complete forgiveness through the Atonement.

f.g: Tread them under foot, like conquered enemies.

f.w: cast all their sins into the depths of the sea

chapters.n: God will keep the promises He made to Abraham and Jacob long ago. Micah ends with confidence in God’s covenant faithfulness.

f.g: Show faithfulness — keep His word.
